about: What a host must do when a checking provider breaks a rule that no schema can express. `run` says how the one run ended. `outcome` is `verdict` with the verdict the host records, or `refused` with the reason. Nothing may be recorded as passed except in the control and in the cases whose outcome is the verdict `passed`. `runs` is how many runs the executor must have been given, no more and no fewer. `deadline_ms`, where given, is the deadline the host is given; `names_a_missing_file` makes the obligation name a file that is not among the inputs. `second_input` gives the check a second input, b.txt; `many_inputs` gives it that many more, so that a request is long; `change_input` breaks one field of the host's own input (null removes it); `names_a_missing_spec` makes the obligation's specified_by name a file that is not among the inputs; `change_input` keys of the form `asked.FIELD` change the whole input's field; `whole_input` replaces the whole input; `non_ascii_input` adds an input named É.txt; `input_text` sends text that is not JSON in its place; `not_on` lists platforms where the provider cannot make what the case needs.

cases.why: A control: a provider that keeps every rule must be accepted, or the other cases prove nothing.
A run that did not exit ends the check in error. The provider is not asked what it thinks.
An executor that cannot be reached is reported as exactly that.
A verdict rests on a run.
A result may not claim more than the manifest declares.
A verdict that states no strength claims one the host cannot bound.
The set of verdicts is closed.
An answer asks for a run or gives a verdict, never both.
An answer that does neither is no answer.
A provider may start only tools it declared.
The same holds for a tool named in an argument.
A program path lies inside the tool it names.
So does a file of a tool named in an argument.
A run starts inside its working directory.
A run writes inside its working directory.
A run may read only what its result is keyed by.
A later run may use only what is in the key.
An answer matches its request.
What a provider says a file contains is never taken on its word.
The same holds for a file it attaches to its verdict: the bytes are hashed again.
An attachment lies inside the working directory.
A check may ask for the same run twice, to see whether a result repeats. Each is submitted under its own key, which includes its number, so the second is never answered from the first.
A tool the manifest declares but the check was not given is not in the key of its result, so a run may not start it.
The same holds for such a tool named in an argument.
A tool named in an argument is a tool named, with or without a file after it.
Every tool named in an argument is looked at, not only the first.
A run uses the tools the check was given, by digest. Another digest is another tool.
The tools a run lists are among those the check was given.
An argument holds no NUL: what follows it would be cut off or read as something else.
A result states the class of strength the manifest declares. A test is not a proof, whatever its rank.
A failure rests on a run as much as a pass does.
The ceiling holds for a failure as for a pass.
An answer carries the id of its request.
The opening echo must come back unchanged, or the two sides do not read text the same way.
A check may ask for eight runs. The ninth is refused before it starts.
A control for the limit: exactly eight runs are allowed.
An argument may not name a file outside the run's own files: an absolute path is refused.
Nor one that climbs out of them.
A run must be given every file its obligation names; a run that reads nothing it was given cannot check anything.
A run must target the platform the check was asked for.
An absolute path inside an option is still outside the run's files.
So is a list of arguments read from another file.
So is a path in a home directory.
So is a URL.
A path glued to a flag is still a path.
So is the parent directory glued to a flag.
A tool file must be the whole argument; anything appended is refused.
A variable can change what a program loads; the stage-0 host allows none.
A run may not write over a file it was given.
A character that only looks like a separator is refused too: a free word may hold printable ASCII only.
An attachment whose bytes have the identity it states is accepted: a host that refuses every attachment would otherwise pass.
A provider may end a check in error after a run; that is a verdict, not a broken rule.
A provider may say at the start that it cannot check this; unsupported needs no run.
A provider that answers a request with an error ends the check; nothing is recorded as a result.
A provider that does not answer within the deadline ends the check.
A run's arguments are a list of strings; a description of the wrong shape is refused before anything else is looked at in it.
The class of strength must match for failed as for passed.
Two rules broken at once: the platform is checked first, so the reason says so.
Two rules broken at once in a final: attachments are checked before the verdict.
A provider that starts a process of its own: when the check ends, that process must be gone too.
An executor that fails and prints nothing ends the check in error; the provider is not asked to interpret it.
An executor that exits well but prints no report ends the check in error.
A report saying the run executed on another platform than it described is an error, never a result.
A report naming another tool digest than the run described is an error, never a result.
An obligation names a file the check was not given; the check is refused before the provider is sent anything.
Outputs that are not a list are not 'no outputs': a path the host never looked at must not reach an executor.
Inputs that are not a list are refused the same way.
A run description lists the tools it uses; one without that list is refused.
Any env field, whatever its value, is refused: null, an empty list and an empty string are not a way round the rule.
An output may not have the path of any of the check's inputs, not only the run's own.
Paths that differ only in letter case are the same file on a disk that ignores case.
An argument holding NUL is refused for that, even where it looks like a tool's file.
A very long time limit is not a reason to end the run at once.
A manifest names each capability once: two strengths for one capability leave the ceiling unknown.
Every capability in a manifest is an object.
A strength rank the scale does not have leaves the ceiling unknown.
A manifest's tools are objects with a name.
A tool's name is letters, digits, dot, underscore and hyphen only, so that ${tool:NAME} can never hide a path.
A provider that stops reading cannot hold the host past its deadline: the deadline covers what the host sends as well as what it waits for.
A final's attachments are a list; anything else is a final of the wrong shape.
A strength without a class does not state the class the manifest declares.
A final is an object.
A next that is not a run description is refused.
An attachment is a regular file: a pipe would hold the host for ever.
An attachment is reached without following a link: a link can lead out of the project.
Strict reading holds inside a body as at the top.
A repeated key inside a nested object is refused as at the top.
An integer beyond plus or minus 2^53-1 cannot be read the same everywhere, and is refused.
A string holding half of a UTF-16 pair is not text.
A result whose body is not an object is not an answer.
A line is read whole before its depth is measured, so a repeated key in it is found first.
An executor's report is read strictly too; one that is not is no report, and the run ended in error.
The host's own input must have the shape the contract gives: an obligation without specified_by is refused, not guessed at.
A tool given to the check without a digest is refused before anything is sent.
An input given to the check without an identity is refused before anything is sent.
An attachment is reached without a symbolic link at any step, even an inner one that leads back inside the project.
An executor that exits with a status other than 0 ends the check in error, even when what it printed reads as a good report.
When the executor returns, every process in its process group or job is gone: a run cannot leave work behind it.
A run's cwd, where given, is a string.
A run's limits, where given, are integers; a number written as a string is not one.
A run's program is an object naming a tool and a path.
The tool a run's program names is a string.
A backslash can join a path on Windows, so an argument holding one must be a file of the run's.
A dollar sign can start a variable a shell or a tool expands.
A percent sign can start a variable on Windows.
The tool a run's program names is in the run's own tools, so the executor pins its digest and reports it.
So is every tool an argument names: a tool missing from the run's tools would run with no digest checked.
A host waits for the executor at least the run's wall_ms plus 60 seconds, however short its own deadline: here the run states 10 seconds and the executor answers after 12.
Each rule is checked over every entry before the next: an unknown tool is found before another tool's wrong digest.
The same holds for inputs: an input not in the key is found before another input's wrong identity.
And for attachments: every path is checked before any identity.
A strength that is given is an object; null is not one.
A manifest's tools is a list; a manifest without one is not read as declaring none.
A final's strength names its class as the manifest does, a string.
Only the host says a check is unavailable, from the executor's report; a provider cannot.
An attachment is an object with a string path and identity.
An attachment holds at most 64 MiB; this one is a byte over, with its true identity.
An answer nested deeper than 64 is refused, after it has been read whole.
NaN is not JSON: an answer holding it is not a message.
An executor's report is read as messages are: a carriage return before its line feed means there is no report.
So does an empty line before it: the first line is the report.
The files that specify an obligation are among the inputs too; one that is not is refused before the provider is sent anything.
The host's own input has its shape: a root that is not a string is refused.
A deadline is a positive integer.
An input without a platform is refused, not given a default.
An input that is not an object is refused, not crashed on.
Input that is not JSON at all is refused like input that is not an object.
A provider's error stays an error whatever reason it gives: only the executor's report makes a check unavailable.
Outputs are compared with inputs ignoring the case of ASCII letters only: é.txt is not É.txt.
A report's tools_ran must be the run's tools; a stray entry is not ignored.
A report whose tools_ran is not a list names no tools, so it is not the run's tools.
